headline: New Hampshire Medicaid premiums remain on hold awaiting federal guidance
dek: A premium system that was expected to start July 1 has no new launch date while the state waits for federal approval and answers about how it fits with new Medicaid cost-sharing rules.
body: New Hampshire’s planned Medicaid premium system remains on hold because the state is still waiting for federal guidance on how the charges would interact with changes made by Congress. The Department of Health and Human Services has not begun collecting the premiums and has not announced a new start date, according to an Oct. 1 report by the [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/01/lacking-federal-approval-new-hampshire-forced-to-hold-off-on-new-medicaid-premiums/).

Jake Leon, a DHHS spokesperson, told the Bulletin that the situation is “status quo” and that the department is still waiting for guidance on the impact of H.R. 1, the federal law commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The premiums had been expected to take effect July 1. The delay means eligible Granite Advantage members are not currently receiving bills under the new system, even though the state law authorizing the charges remains in place.

New Hampshire law directs DHHS to seek a Medicaid waiver and, if necessary, a state-plan amendment to charge premiums to Granite Advantage participants with household income at or above 100% of the federal poverty level. The statute sets monthly amounts of $60 for a one-person household, $80 for two people, $90 for three people and $100 for a household of four or more during the biennium ending June 30, 2027. It also requires the department to develop hardship criteria. The [New Hampshire General Court’s text of RSA 126-AA:2-a](https://gc.nh.gov/rsa/html/X/126-AA/126-AA-2-a.htm) makes the charges subject to federal limits on cost sharing and eligibility.

That federal condition is central to the delay. Medicaid is jointly administered by the states and the federal government, so New Hampshire needs approval from the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services before the premium structure can operate. The Bulletin reported that state officials have been weighing whether the planned premiums can coexist with H.R. 1 provisions that create cost sharing for some Medicaid enrollees. The law’s cost-sharing provisions are scheduled to take effect in 2028, but the state is waiting for the federal government to clarify how the programs should be coordinated before it spends money to launch the collection system.

A DHHS presentation to state lawmakers lists the conflict in its implementation timeline. The agency’s [Medicaid Changes from HR 1 document](https://gc.nh.gov/statstudcomm/committees/72/documents/Medicaid%20Changes%20from%20HR%201.pdf) says the state budget requires Granite Advantage premiums in state fiscal year 2027, while the federal cost-sharing requirement is scheduled for Oct. 1, 2028. The same document says DHHS planned to submit a waiver by July 1, 2026; the current status reported by the department’s spokesperson shows that submission has not yet produced an approved launch path.

The policy would affect more than a small administrative group. The [New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute](https://nhfpi.org/resource/the-state-budget-for-fiscal-years-2026-and-2027/) estimated that about 11,000 adults in Granite Advantage would be subject to the adult premiums. Its review of the state budget said monthly charges would range from $60 to $100 depending on household size. The budget also includes a separate premium structure for households with children enrolled through the Children’s Health Insurance Program, with monthly amounts ranging from $190 to $270 for families above the applicable income threshold.

Supporters have described the premiums as a way to preserve broad eligibility while generating revenue for the program. Opponents argue that even modest monthly charges can discourage enrollment or care, especially for people whose incomes sit just above the poverty line. A [New Hampshire legislative analysis](https://gc.nh.gov/bill_status/legacy/bs2016/HearingReport.aspx?id=11706&sy=2026) of a bill that would have repealed the premiums recorded both the planned July 1 start for Medicaid expansion enrollees and the concern that the state could spend on a collection system that federal law may soon make obsolete. The bill was later listed as inexpedient to legislate and did not become the current governing law.

For now, the practical answer for Granite Advantage members is that the new premiums have not started. The next major decision belongs to DHHS and federal Medicaid officials: they must determine whether the state can secure approval, revise the design or wait for the federal cost-sharing framework. Until that process produces a new authorization and timeline, New Hampshire residents should not assume that the amounts listed in state law are current bills or that a launch date has been set.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire Medicaid premiums delayed pending federal approval
seoDescription: New Hampshire has not started planned Medicaid premiums while DHHS awaits federal guidance and approval on how the charges fit with new cost-sharing rules.
